speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I want to talk a little bit about the state of AI now and where we think it's going.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But before diving into that, I just want to do a brief kind of like tour over the past few years because it seems like things move so fast.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But only like three years ago was when all of this kind of like really kicked off.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Actually, a little bit before that was when LangChain launched.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In 2023, we were building prototypes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In 2024, we were shipping some of these simple applications to production, but they were still like single LLM calls.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: 2025, we started exploring agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And really this year, we've started seeing that agents have transformed the application layer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so a lot of the talks that you'll hear from today are companies that are doing exactly that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They're taking these LLMs and they're really building them into differentiated experiences.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So it's not just the model that they're providing to their customers, it's everything around the model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we're seeing that these domain-specific agents, they're not just wrappers, they're providing real value to folks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And people are having to build
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A lot of things around the model to properly take advantage of that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so calling out a few, so Rogo, we'll do a fireside chat with them later today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They had a great blog where they wrote about how they built a specialized harness with model routing to provide a domain-specific agent for finance.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Harvey, who we heard from at some previous interrupts, has been talking a lot about how they've fine-tuned models for specialized tasks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They had the best performance on legal domain.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then JPMorgan Chase, we'll hear from them later today, a little bit of a different use case, internal use case, but customizing the harness around the model to provide a lot of internal advantages for the agents that they're building as part of their Jarvis assembly line.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So all of these are examples of companies taking the model, building a lot of stuff around it to make it truly theirs, and the phrase that has been going around to really exemplify all of this is owning your intelligence.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When we talk about owning your intelligence, we talk about all of these examples basically building a lot of domain-specific things in and around the models to make it truly best for the domain that you're trying to tackle and really owning your intelligence.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we think there's a few reasons why this has become a phrase that's top of mind for so many people these days.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First, token costs are rising a lot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: People are spending more and more on AI and so as they do so they want to make sure that they're getting the proper ROI and being able to control and monitor token costs is really important and so owning your intelligence in that regard is a key factor.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Second, we see open models becoming more and more popular.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this provides not only a really cheap alternative in order to own the token costs more, but it also lets you customize things more.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so as these base open weight models get better and better, you can start to post train them, you can start to use them in specialized ways, and that just makes it easier than ever to really own your intelligence.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then the last thing that I think has become pretty clear over the past year is that the models themselves are becoming somewhat commoditized and it's all of this stuff around the model, in particular the data, whether that is actual kind of like context you're providing or some of the domain specific paths that you're baking into the harness,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is becoming the differentiator to provide a lot of value for folks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so because of all of these factors, we're seeing people want to own their intelligence more and more, and that's how we think about our mission as a company.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's always been this way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: LangChain got started a month before ChatGPT, but really took off after.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When people saw that came out, and they were like, I want that, but for my industry, for my vertical,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then a big value prop of LinkedIn has always been kind of like model optionality.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so from the beginning, people were building these domain-specific things that were naturally kind of like decoupled from the model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so this mission of kind of like owning intelligence has been something we've thought a lot about.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we think there's three core pillars to this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is what we help folks with.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the first core pillar is open and controllable harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so there's two kind of like key parts to this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One, we think the harness needs to be model neutral, so you shouldn't be coupled to a particular model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is both offensive and defensive.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When the best new model comes out, whether it's from OpenAI or Anthropic or TypeSafe with some of their dev models, you want to be able to switch your harness to that as quickly as possible.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so your harness needs to be able to adapt to the best new model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's also defensive.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You don't want to get locked into a single model provider so that they can raise rates and things like that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The other part of this open and controllable harness is, again, what we talked about in terms of making these agents really domain-specific.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: All of that is about bringing specialized context in particular ways to the model to bring it the right context at the right point in time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you need to really control what the harness does.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what that control looks like could look different for different scenarios.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we've had LangGraph for a while, which is an open source framework for really creating these directed graphs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's a really controllable way of bringing this harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We also have deep agents now, and I'll talk about that later, but that's another kind of open source model harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have a concept of middleware in there, which is a different way of injecting decisions to make and things to do into this core agentic loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so regardless of what it is, you need a way to control really in real detail what's going in to the model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The second core pillar that we think makes up owning your intelligence
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: is compounding, specifically compounding the intelligence that you get from when people use your system.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So when you launch an agent, that is far from having a successful agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You need to learn from how people use the agent, what the agent does, see where it makes mistakes, and being able to compound that agent's intelligence, whether manually by seeing errors and updating the code or updating the prompt,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Or more automatically, whether that's with memory or prompt optimization things, this compounding loop is really important to build into your systems and to own.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you can define what better and what best looks like for your domain better than anyone else, you will be able to build the best agent for that domain.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so having evals that define what good looks like and then hill climbing on those evals and compounding that intelligence is a really good way to build these domain-specific agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then lastly, governed.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is really crucial for internal agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We're seeing a ton of companies transform how they do internal operations, but when you have a lot of agents running around, you need to make sure that they're properly governed.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You need to make sure that you know how many exist, that you can control costs, that you can handle off reliably, so different people accessing it only have access to what they should have access to.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we see that governance is becoming an increasingly big topic around owning your intelligence.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so this is how we think about the three core pillars of owning intelligence.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we think there's a bunch of different ways that you can get there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so calling three out at a high level, people, process, and technology.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we're going to talk most about technology during the rest of the keynote.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But I want to touch really briefly on people and process, because those are also needed to transform your organization into an organization that can own its intelligence.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So touching really briefly on people, this is roughly how we see a lot of organizations being built.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's a ring one of like core platform engineers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: These provide a lot of tools for other people to build agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When we talk about governance, when we talk about this kind of like eval compounding loop, these provide the platform that other
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Agent building teams internally can use to build and govern and compound their agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Outside of that, we see agent engineers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is a great term to describe the weird hybrid mix of data scientist and engineer and machine learning engineer that makes up the people who are driving these agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it's a new skill set.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we see a lot of people from different disciplines coming in to be agent engineers, consuming things from the core platform team
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then lastly, there are a ton of subject matter experts inside and outside the company who are often the best people to decide what good looks like for an agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so having a platform that can touch those non-developers at the edges is super important.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so people and kind of like setting up your organization
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Have this type of model is what we see people doing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We also see people either implicitly or explicitly adopting a kind of like new process for building agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As I mentioned before, it's very iterative.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You first launch an agent, it's not going to be good.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You need to iterate.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so there's this lifecycle, this loop that people are adopting.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In order to really get agents to be good enough, roughly speaking, it's build, test, deploy, monitor, and then crucially when you take those monitor learnings and you bring them back into the build step.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And of course you want to do all of this in a governed way, and we'll come back to this a little bit later, but people are doing this type of process all the time to improve their agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then I want to talk about the technology.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And when we think about the technology and the technology that we help build and provide, there's really like two core parts to it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So one is the runtime.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is how we got started with the open source LangChain libraries and continue to do open source things with LangGraph and DeepAgents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then, of course, we want to build agents that don't just run locally on your laptop, but run in the cloud and can serve everyone inside your org or the customers that you're building for.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so there's a deployment aspect to this runtime as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then there's this observability and evals part, which is really crucial for the compounding layer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so being able to see what agents are doing and measure how good they are behaving is really important.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So these are the two core pillars of things that we build.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And recently we've also focused on a third part, which is an intelligence layer that sits above them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So now when we think about LangSmith, our commercial platform, we think about it serving the runtime aspect, serving the observability evals aspect, and then building an intelligence across the platform to really help people utilize these components and speed up that process, that agent development lifecycle that I talked about earlier.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so for the next few minutes, I want to walk through these kind of like three core parts of our platform and talk about some of the cool things that we're doing and where we think the future is going.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I want to start with runtime.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so what is the runtime for kind of like an agent look like?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When we think of an agent, we generally think of there being three components.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's the business logic.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is things like instructions, tools, skills, hooks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: These are things that you guys have to provide when you're building your domain-specific agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What skills for a financial agent might look like are very different than what skills for a legal agent might look like.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so this is the business logic that everyone out here will provide to the agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then there's the harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so the harness is what takes the model, takes a lot of this domain-specific context, and basically wires it all up so that the model can see the right context at the right point in time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This can be a very kind of like custom harness that you might build in LangGraph.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Or it can be a more kind of like general purpose harness, which we're seeing more and more of.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so that's why we built DeepAgents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so DeepAgents is our newest open source library.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We launched it about a year ago.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's off the shelf agent harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It learns a lot from what coding agents do.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So it has an execution environment with a file system in sandbox.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It does a lot of context management in ways that coding agents do it with compaction.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But it's built so that you can build these domain specific agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then lastly, there's the infrastructure.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so if you take this agent and it's running locally on your laptop, great.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You want to bring it to the cloud.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's all of these components that you're going to need to add in so that it can run remotely.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You'll want a runtime in a server that has durable execution.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You'll want some way to access tools securely.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You'll want some way to run this code that it writes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we see a lot of agents writing code, even if they're not coding agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You'll need to access models.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so there's all this infrastructure that goes into it as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so these are a lot of the components that we've built into LangSmith in pieces.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we have LangSmith deployments.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's really around the agent runtime.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have LangSmith sandboxes for running codes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In beta, we have an LLM gateway in LangSmith, and I'll talk about that, but that's for access to models.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then a tool server is something that we're working on for easy access to tools.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so there's these different components that make up the infrastructure.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And one of the things that we launched in beta at last interrupt, but I want to spotlight real quick, is managed deep agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So managed deep agents basically takes this harness and the managed infrastructure and combines it into one.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so now when you're building an agent,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You just provide your business logic and then you get the harness and managed infrastructure together.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so that's a lot easier to get started with than having to go business logic to harness to assembling all these three or four or five different pieces of infrastructure.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we're really, really excited about the managed deep agents platform as a way to accelerate time to value and speed to kind of like production for a lot of these agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's a few things that we're announcing today as part of a new Managed Deep Agents release that we think will help even more with this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So first, one of the hardest parts of building these, especially internal company agents, is auth and making sure that the right people can access and use the agent, but also that when they use the agent, if the agent connects to Notion or Jira,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's connecting either on behalf of the user or as the agent's kind of fixed set of identity.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then what the right answer is might depend.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we're introducing a lot of different primitives in managed deep agents to facilitate this type of connections.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So first is connections.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: These are basically tools.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When you have a tool server, which is how Managed Deep Agents connects to tools, you can specify how you want your end users to auth to those connections.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we're using auth there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Related to that, we have this idea of identity for agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This just defines the agent to be either user-permissioned or service-permissioned on a whole.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then third is channels.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So a big part of building these agents is exposing them to people.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Slack is a massive one.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When you have agents in Slack,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How do you deal with auth in like a shared channel?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If I message it in a shared public channel and my coworker messages it, whose auth does it use?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For which runs?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A lot of that we're baking in to off-the-shelf channels and manage deep agents to hopefully make the auth problem a lot easier.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Second, we're adding more things around memory into managed deep agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so managed deep agents has always had a concept of agent level memory, but we're now adding in user level memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this means that it can remember things specific to the individual users that it interacts with.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is really powerful for customizing agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then third, we're adding in built-in tools.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So one of the most common things that agents need to do is search the web.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we're adding in a built-in tool via parallel so that agents can access the web.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so now you no longer have to go get a separate API key for that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can just use your LangSmith API key, use it with managed deep agents, and get access to the parallel web search MCP.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so putting this all together, managed deep agents we think is the easiest way to go from the business logic to an agent that's actually running in production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We've been working with a number of early design partners on this, and we've seen really good results, especially for just getting an agent up and running and having it be like this company harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's how we think about managed deep agents, is this company harness that makes it really easy to get started building and sharing agents inside an org.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The next thing in the runtime that I want to spotlight is decision models.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so over the weekend, I, as I'm sure many of you did, played around with Jev.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So it launched over the weekend.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a really interesting new type of model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a decision model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What does that mean?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It basically means that it makes decisions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You send it a state.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You send it a list of questions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It can then score those questions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And there's different things that you can have it score on.

text: So it can either be like a Boolean or an actual score or a categorical choice.

text: But it basically makes decisions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so even though it's more limited, we think this is really interesting.

text: We think there are a bunch of different types of models and a bunch of different types of agent harnesses that will be built.

text: And that's what you're going to use in Claude Code and Codex and DeepAgents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: These take advantage.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: of these really frontier models.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But there's also a ton of other decisions that need to be made, and that's where we think a decision model can be really helpful.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And maybe these are small things that actually go along with the frontier model, or maybe they empower the lane graph cognitive architectures and routing between different things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so calling out a few of the things that we think these decision models are really useful, one is evals, so either running after the fact or in the loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you have an agent doing work, if you can score it quickly,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: According to some criteria as it's running, that's really powerful because then you can catch mistakes in real time.

text: Two, guardrails.

text: So flagging user input really fast.

text: So I was talking to some people yesterday and we were talking about guardrails.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One of the downsides of guardrails is that it always adds latency.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we're excited about it for that.

text: And then lastly, model routing as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Speaking really quickly of our gateway, this is the last thing in the runtime that I want to spotlight.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we launched LangSmith's LLM gateway in beta about a month or two ago.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's two main things that I want to highlight.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One, we try to make it so that the gateway can be used in all of the LLM applications that you're building, whether they are customer-facing or internal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So specifically, we normalize everything through OpenAI and actually Anthropic message format.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you can access it there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But we also allow straight pass-through in case there are new features that come out in these APIs and you just want to take advantage of.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then we also have a bunch of coding agent integrations.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So Codex and Claude Code and Cursor, again, we think you should be routing all of your traffic for governance and cost control reasons.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We think you should be routing all of it through a single element gateway.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so that means it needs to integrate with every application that's using AI.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we want to make it so really easy to plug into all of those.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then the main kind of like features that we're focusing on, one is cost controls, having cost visibility but also setting spend limits for different teams, different users, different API keys.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Two is rate limiting, so making sure that there's not a single application that's really throttling or taking up a lot of usage there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then third is fallbacks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you can fall back to different model providers when you get an error.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then one of the things that we'll be launching soon is actually more stateful fallbacks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So if you notice that requests are failing and Anthropic might be down, you don't even try them for the future.
speaker: SPEAKER_00
